title: Why do two folds give a line parallel to l?
description: A crease l and a point are given on a sheet of paper. One fold makes a crease through the point at a right angle to l, and a second fold makes a crease through the point at a right angle to the first. The two right angles are compared, and Keeko doubts that one fold is enough.
teaching_notes: One idea: two lines that are both perpendicular to the same line make equal corresponding angles of ninety degrees, so they are parallel. Watch for students who think any single crease through the point is parallel to l.

source: A crease l and a point A are given. Fold a line m through A
video_script.why: The child sees that two folds at right angles to the same crease give equal corresponding angles, so the creases are parallel.
video_script.substitution: the book's own paper folding: a crease l, a point A, a crease t through A, and a crease m through A
video_script.anchor: a sheet of paper with a crease l and a point A, folded to make a crease t and then a crease m, both through A
video_script.wrong_move: believes any single crease through the point is parallel to l, and skips the second fold
video_script.payoff_line: Equal corresponding angles make the lines parallel

final_answer.value: m is parallel to l, since both are perpendicular to t, so the corresponding angles are both 90°
final_answer.spoken: m is parallel to l, since both are perpendicular to t, so the corresponding angles are both ninety degrees

maths_rules: first fold: l falls on itself, the crease t passes through A, so t is perpendicular to l
second fold: t falls on itself, the crease m passes through A, so m is perpendicular to t
t crosses l at 90 degrees and crosses m at 90 degrees, and these are corresponding angles
90 = 90, so the corresponding angles are equal and l and m are parallel
video_script.design: One sheet of paper, the crease l, the point A, then t folded through A and m folded through A. The two right angles of t with l and with m are marked in one colour.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks one fold is enough, and any crease through eigh is parallel to l.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But a crease through eigh can lean any way, and most of them would cross l.
<bookmark mark='second'/>The second fold makes a right angle with t, and that makes the corresponding angles equal.
